what_it_does: Modern computers run on steady wall-power, but some tiny devices — like wireless sensors or medical implants — harvest energy from their environment (light, radio waves, body heat) and can lose power at any moment. When power cuts out, the device's short-term memory (the cache, a small fast store of recently-used data) loses whatever it was holding. Existing tricks for saving energy by switching off unused parts of the cache were designed for always-on machines and don't account for these sudden losses, so they waste power keeping data alive that will vanish before it can ever be used. This paper adds a power-failure-aware prediction layer — called EDBP (Enhanced Dead Block Predictor) — on top of existing cache-management logic. EDBP estimates when the next power cut is likely and proactively switches off cache regions that probably won't be touched before then, cutting the slow trickle of 'leakage' energy those regions consume and freeing that energy for actual computation.
